reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
The material for defense is mostly about the machinery of federal procurement rather than about measured AI adoption. SAM.gov is described as the government's own system of record for federal contract opportunities, awards, and vendor registrations, free and searchable, and the page text harvested from it is dominated by administrative notices, including revisions to subcontracting plan reporting eligibility logic, changes to wage determination formatting, and the retirement of the FPDS.gov ezSearch feature, with users directed to conduct contract award searches in SAM.gov instead. The Federal Procurement Data System is described as recording DoD contract actions and vendor performance history at the transaction level, and the FPDS.gov page confirms that the ATOM Feed will be retired later in FY 2026 and that subcontracting reporting capabilities have moved into SAM.gov following the retirement of eSRS.gov. USAspending is named as the place where every federal award is downloadable, built on the Federal Procurement Data System feed, so contract spending on AI-related solutions traces there.

The Defense Innovation Unit appears as the commercial on-ramp, described in the curated points as where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings, and its own page states the mission as converting entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power. Govini is described as a defense-intelligence platform used inside the Department that tracks procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy and publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending, and its page text describes a platform layer that turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. Janes is presented as a long-running defense analysis provider maintaining databases of contractors, programs, and procurement forecasts, a subscription source named for completeness, and its page describes validated open source defence and security intelligence, human collection by vetted specialists, peer review, and a dataset it calls the largest global dataset of its type.

On government AI labs, the catalogued page counts two individually verified organisations, each with a sourced classification note, and names the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi, operating under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and having published frontier open models, and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China, described as a state-established research institution backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government. The page's own framing is that state-funded government labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which shapes what they build and why, and that both institutions can in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.

Several things a reader might expect are not in this material. There is no measured adoption figure for defense, and no Census Bureau figure is present. There is no ROI evidence reported by any source here. The Silicon Valley Defense Group is listed in the curated points as a nonprofit monitoring the intersection of commercial tech, private capital, and national security and publicly mapping companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space, but the page text harvested from its site is in German and concerns a recruitment agency for values-oriented companies, so it supports nothing about defense AI and should not be leaned on. The curated description of what this page covers names decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record, but the excerpts themselves do not detail those programs.

For someone deciding whether to deploy, the practical takeaway from this material is about where the evidence lives rather than what it says. The free federal sources, SAM.gov, FPDS, and USAspending, are the places to look for AI-related solicitations, awards, and vendor history, and the curated points treat them as the first stop, with subscription analysts such as Janes labeled as such. DIU is identified as the route by which commercial products enter Department programs, and Govini as a platform used inside the Department for procurement and supply-chain analysis. Beyond that, the sources here describe capability and intent, not results, and a deployment decision would need evidence this material does not contain.

https://www.svdg.org/.brief: The page presents Motiv, an agency run by Andrej Schindler and Jonas von der Gathen that describes itself as an "Agentur für Zukunftspotenziale", placing creative people with values-oriented companies. It says it connects people and companies, accompanies individual development and creates space for future perspectives, driven by curiosity about people and how organisations evolve. Companies are described as grown, unique organisms whose sense of purpose and urge to develop are their driving forces, and the agency says its aim is to place people who bring both professional expertise and the ability to connect with a company's purpose. It states that it works with companies holding social and ecological values and seeks long-term working relationships, and that it sees people as developing beings whose individual potential it tries to recognise at the right moment for a career step. The page also invites readers to register for a quarterly newsletter with open positions, accounts of company visits and interviews.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The World of AI catalogues two organisations it classifies as government labs, each verified individually against a document the organisation published about itself, with the deciding source and the date it was last read recorded. It describes Shanghai AI Laboratory as a state-established Chinese research institution backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government, and says Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has published frontier open models. The site argues that state-funded labs hold a distinct position because they carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which shapes what they build. It adds that both entries, despite sharing the classification, represent very different political economies, and that both can in principle command infrastructure commitments such as compute and facilities that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.
